title: Sufi Tales of the Heart
description: The Sufis never argued. They told stories and they danced. The whirling that turns around a still centre, Mulla Nasruddin searching for the donkey he is sitting on, Rabia running through the streets with fire and water, the king's ring that said: this too shall pass, and the moth that loved the flame. Then a gentle turning meditation.

beats.say: The Sufis are the mystics of the heart. They don't argue about God. They don't build big systems of philosophy. They tell jokes, they sing, they dance in circles until they disappear.
People thought they were mad. And they were, a little. Mad with love.
Their stories travelled from Persia to India, from caravan to caravan, from tea house to tea house. Nobody knows who first told them. They belong to everyone.
So sit back, as if you are in an old tea house in the evening, and listen.
The dervishes of Konya, the friends of Rumi, discovered a strange meditation. They turn. Round and round, with one hand raised to the sky and the other turned down to the earth.
What comes from above, they say, passes through the heart and goes into the earth. They keep nothing for themselves. They are only a hollow reed.
If you watch them, you see something beautiful. The body is turning fast, the skirts are flying... and the face is completely calm.
Like a wheel. The rim is moving fast, but the centre of the wheel is still. They have found the still centre in the middle of the turning.
Your life is turning too. Office, home, family, bills, round and round. You don't need to stop the wheel. You need to find the centre.
And when the turning stops, the dervish falls to the earth, and lies there like a child in its mother's lap. Utterly empty. Utterly at home.
One morning the whole village saw Mulla Nasruddin galloping through the market on his donkey, shouting: Has anyone seen my donkey? I have lost my donkey!
He went from shop to shop, from street to street, asking everyone. The people were laughing so much they could not answer him.
Finally an old man stopped him. Mulla, he said, you are sitting on your donkey! Nasruddin looked down, very surprised. So I am, he said. Thank God! I was so worried.
The whole village laughed for a week. And Nasruddin laughed with them, because he had done it on purpose.
We are all galloping on the donkey we are searching for. We are searching for happiness, for God, for peace... and we are sitting on it.
Stop. Look down. What you are looking for is the very thing that is looking.
Rabia was one of the greatest of the Sufis. A woman, poor, once a slave, and so full of love that even the great scholars of Basra came to sit at her feet.
One day the people saw her running through the streets. In one hand she carried a burning torch. In the other, a bucket of water.
Rabia, what are you doing? they asked. And she said: I am going to burn down paradise with this fire, and drown hell with this water.
So that people stop loving God out of fear of hell, or out of greed for heaven. So that they love only for the sake of love.
Look at our prayers. Give me this, protect me from that. They are business deals. A little fear, a little greed, dressed up as religion.
Another time, Rabia was searching for something on the road outside her hut. A needle, she said. I dropped it inside, but the light is better out here.
The scholars laughed at her. And she said: you are doing the same. You lost God inside, and you are searching outside, in books and in pilgrimages, because outside there is more light.
Strange. The same story we tell about Mulla Nasruddin and his key, she told about the needle. Truth keeps coming back in new clothes, until somebody listens.
Rabia's prayer was different. She asked for nothing. She only said: let me love you, and that is enough. That is the heart of the Sufi way.
A great king once called all the wise men of his kingdom and said: Make me a ring. And on it write something that will help me when I am in despair... and also when I am too happy.
The wise men argued for weeks. Nothing satisfied them. Finally an old Sufi, who had been sitting quietly in the corner, gave the king a small ring.
On it were four words. This too shall pass.
Years later the king lost a war. His army was destroyed, his kingdom taken. He was hiding in a cave, alone, ready to kill himself. Then he looked at his ring. This too shall pass.
And it passed. He gathered his people again, and won his kingdom back. There was a great festival, music, dancing, the king drunk with victory... and then he looked at the ring.
This too shall pass. And the king became quiet, and humble, in the middle of his success.
Everything passes. Pain and pleasure, praise and blame. Only one thing does not pass: the one who watches them come and go.
The villagers asked Mulla Nasruddin to give a sermon at the mosque. He climbed up and said: Do you know what I am going to tell you? No, said the people. We have no idea.
Then I will not waste my time on such ignorant people, said Nasruddin. And he went home.

The next week they asked again. Do you know what I am going to tell you? This time the people were clever. Yes, they said, we know. Then there is no need for me to tell you, said Nasruddin, and he went home.
The third week they had a plan. Do you know what I am going to tell you? Half the people shouted yes, and the other half shouted no.
Wonderful, said Nasruddin. Then those who know can tell those who don't know. And he went home.
We laugh at him. But he is saying something very deep. Truth cannot be given in a sermon. Those who know, know. Those who don't, must find it for themselves.
No mosque, no temple, no teacher can do your seeing for you. At most, a finger can point.
The Sufi poet Attar tells of some moths who wanted to know the truth about the flame. The first moth flew near a candle in a window, came back and said: it is bright.
The second moth flew closer, burned its wings a little, came back and said: it is hot. But the wise old moth said: neither of you knows anything.
Then the third moth flew straight into the flame, and became one with it, and burned up completely. And the old moth said: only he knows. But he cannot come back to tell us.
This is what the Sufis mean by love. Not standing at a safe distance and admiring the light. Falling into it, and disappearing.
It sounds frightening. But what burns is only the small self, the ego, the little moth with its opinions. What remains is the flame.
Now let us try a small turning. If you have space, stand up. Raise one hand gently, and begin to turn slowly on the spot, the way a child turns in the garden.
Keep the eyes soft and open. Don't look at anything. Let the world become a blur of colour and light around you.
And feel... the centre of your body is not moving. Everything turns around it. Stay with that still point in the belly.
Now slowly, slowly, let the turning come to a stop. And sit down, or lie down on the earth. Close your eyes.
The world is still turning inside you. Let it turn. Feel the earth holding you. You are a small child on its mother's breast.
Feel the heart. Let it be open, like a door left open in the evening for anyone to come in.
There is nothing to do now. The dance has done its work. Rest in the stillness that it left behind.
And when you are ready, take a deep breath, and open your eyes. May your heart stay a little open today, my friend.
